candidates.quote: Underlying all these developments is the realisation that being explicit about effects is extremely useful, and this is something that we believe may ultimately be seen as one of Haskell’s main impacts on mainstream programming
candidates.statement: Keep the language pure and make every effect explicit in the type of a computation.

strongest.why: it is a stance on how one should program: effects are a discipline to be controlled and made visible, not a default

also.why: it opens infinite data structures and unusual control flow as ordinary values

harms: space leaks that are hard to anticipate
operational behaviour opaque, so profiling and debugging are hard

candidates.quote: Lazy evaluation—with its direct connection to the pure, call-by-name lambda calculus, the remarkable possibility of representing and manipulating infinite data structures, and addictively simple and beautiful implementation techniques—was like a drug.
candidates.statement: Evaluate lazily, so that evaluation order follows need and infinite structures are ordinary values.

strongest.why: the designers describe lazy evaluation as addictive, "like a drug", the thing that drew them in

candidates.above_next: it reframes what a program is, but rests on the purity already stated above

also.why: the economy of reading code as mathematics over a known domain

beats.why: l172's minimal surfaces is an evocative image but vaguer; executable mathematics names a precise, usable reframing

harms: sets an ideal the language rarely fully meets
candidates.quote: Because of referential transparency, Haskell programs can be viewed as executable mathematics, as equations over the category of complete partial orders. In principle, at least, the specification becomes the program.
candidates.statement: Because of referential transparency a program can be read as executable mathematics, equations whose specification is the program.

strongest.why: it recasts a program as a system of equations, so the specification can be the program

also.why: a single pattern unifies state, exceptions, parsing, I/O and more

harms: monads do not compose in a modular way

a steep learning curve for newcomers
candidates.quote: The key idea is to treat a value of type IO a as a “computation” that, when performed, might perform input and output before delivering a value of type a.

strongest.why: it turns an effectful computation into a first-class value you can build and sequence

candidates.above_next: type classes reorganise polymorphism, but infect a narrower slice of thought than computations do

also.why: one mechanism cleanly captures equality, ordering, numbers, show/read and more

harms: dynamic semantics depends on how overloading is resolved
the design grew into chaotic complexity
candidates.quote: They were originally proposed early in the design process, by Wadler and Blott ... as a ... principled solution to a relatively small problem (operator overloading for numeric operations and equality).
candidates.statement: Resolve ad-hoc overloading in a principled way through type classes, constraints that qualify a polymorphic type.

strongest.why: a principled account of overloading as bounded quantification, a predicate over types

candidates.above_next: DSELs turn the language outward into domains, a reach slightly less central than the class system

also.why: it argues the way to attack a domain is to build its language rather than a program in a fixed one

harms: the embedded language inherits the host's error messages
a leaky abstraction when host semantics intrudes (e.g. sharing)
candidates.quote: the idea of writing a library that turns Haskell into a domainspecific embedded language (DSEL), a term first coined by Hudak
candidates.statement: Write a library that turns the language into a domain-specific embedded language sharing its syntax, types and tools.

strongest.why: a library becomes a language, so writing a program is designing its vocabulary

also.why: a stance that the user interface of a language, its syntax, deserves first-class care

beats.why: l116's succinctness is a benefit; wanting the surface to look like mathematics is the design commitment that produces it

harms: notation debates consume disproportionate effort (Wadler's law)

strongest.why: making code read like mathematics is pursued for the beauty and economy of the surface itself
